name: Guhyeshwari Temple
deity: Guhyeshwari (Guhyakali), a form of the Great Goddess; consort of Pashupati
significance: A Shakta pitha on the southern bank of the Bagmati inside the Pashupatinath precinct of Kathmandu, and one of the most important shrines in Nepal for Tantric practitioners. King Pratap Malla is credited with renovating it in the 17th century.
story: Tradition holds that the goddess Sati's rectum fell here when Shiva carried her body across the earth; Vajrayana Buddhists identify the same spot with Vajrayogini and with the root of the mythical lotus that bore the Swayambhu stupa.

name: Jeshoreshwari Kali Temple
deity: Kali as Jeshoreshwari (Bhairava: Chanda)
builtDisplay: c. 1600 (Pratapaditya); natmandir renovated earlier under Lakshman Sen
significance: An old Kali shrine at Ishwaripur in Satkhira district, counted among the 51 Shakta pithas as the place where Sati's palm fell. Its present form is associated with Maharaja Pratapaditya of Jessore, with earlier renovation attributed to Lakshman Sen.
story: A general of Pratapaditya is said to have followed a beam of light into the bushes and found a stone carved in the shape of a human palm, whereupon the king raised a temple to Kali on the spot.

name: Kiriteswari Temple
deity: Devi Kiriteshwari (Mukuteshwari / Mahishamardini)
significance: A Shakta pitha in Murshidabad district said to be over a thousand years old, destroyed in 1405 and rebuilt in the 19th century by Darpanarayan, king of Lalgola. It was named India's Best Tourism Village in 2023.
story: The crown (kirit) of Sati is believed to have fallen here after her self-immolation, giving the shrine and the village their name.

name: Nainativu Nagapooshani Amman Temple
deity: Parvati as Nagapooshani (Bhuvaneswari), with Shiva as Nayinaar
significance: The principal Hindu temple of Nainativu island off the Jaffna peninsula, counted among the Shakta pithas of the goddess and a major cultural landmark for Sri Lankan Tamils. The present temple was raised between 1720 and 1790 after the Portuguese destroyed the earlier shrine in 1620.
story: The temple's name derives from Naka, the cobra, reflecting a long local tradition of serpent worship on the island.

name: Nalateswari Temple
deity: Kalika as Nalateshwari
significance: A Shakta pitha shrine in the Birbhum town of Nalhati, which takes its name from the temple. It is counted among the 51 seats of the goddess and draws pilgrims from across Bengal.
story: The nala, or throat, of the goddess Shakti is said to have fallen at this spot.

name: Nartiang Durga Temple
deity: Durga as Jainteshwari (Bhairava: Kamadishwar)
significance: A roughly 600-year-old Shakta pitha in the West Jaintia Hills, established under the Jaintia king Jaso Manik and regarded as the goddess's permanent seat in north-east India. It draws large crowds of pilgrims at Durga Puja.
story: The goddess is said to have appeared to King Jaso Manik in a dream asking for a temple at the place where Sati's left thigh had fallen.

name: Vishalakshi Temple
deity: Vishalakshi, an aspect of Parvati
significance: A Shakta pitha near Mir Ghat in Varanasi, rebuilt in 1893 by the Nattukottai Nagarathar merchant community of Tamil Nadu. It is one of the most venerated goddess shrines of the city and a focus of devotion for Tamil pilgrims.
story: The earrings of Sati are said to have fallen at this spot in Varanasi.

name: Devi Talab Mandir
deity: Durga, with shrines to Kali and Shiva
significance: A Shakta pitha temple built beside an old tank in Jalandhar, richly finished in gold work and drawing thousands of pilgrims each year. The complex also holds a replica of the Amarnath shrine.

name: Vimala Temple
deity: Vimala (Bimala), the tantric form of Lakshmi
dynasty: Eastern Ganga (also attributed to Somavamshi Yayati Keshari)
significance: The goddess shrine inside the Jagannath Temple complex at Puri, dated to the 9th century and built in four-part Kalinga form. It is a Shakta pitha and the ritual heart of Tantric worship within an otherwise Vaishnava sanctuary.
story: Parvati complained to Vishnu that she had lost her rightful share of offerings, and he promised she would dwell at Puri as Vimala and receive the remnants of Jagannath's food in the Kali Yuga.

name: Thanumalayan (Sthanumalayan) Temple, Suchindram
deity: Sthanumalayan, the Trimurti of Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma in a single linga
dynasty: Chola, later Madurai Nayak and Travancore
style: Dravidian with Kerala and Tamil elements
significance: A large temple at Suchindram in Kanyakumari district revered by both Shaiva and Vaishnava traditions, unusual for enshrining all three members of the Trimurti in one linga. Its masonry structure dates from the Chola period, with a 44 m eleven-storey eastern gopuram added under later patrons.
story: Anasuya, wife of the sage Atri, is said to have turned Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva into infants by the power of her chastity, after which the three emanated here as lingas.

name: Nandikeshwari Temple, Sainthia
deity: Nandikeshwari, the goddess worshipped by Nandi
significance: A Shakta pitha at Sainthia in Birbhum whose present temple was raised in 1913. Its history is tied to the tradition of Sati's self-sacrifice at her father's ritual.
story: The collarbone of Sati's body is said to have fallen here after Vishnu's discus dismembered it to calm Shiva's grief.

name: Bargabhima Temple
deity: Devi Bargabhima (Kapalini / Bhimarupa), a form of Kali
style: Blend of Bengali Hindu and Buddhist forms
significance: A Shakti shrine at Tamluk, the ancient port of Tamralipta, built by the Tamluk Raj family and rebuilt after the medieval Islamic conquest of Bengal. It later served as a gathering point where freedom fighters took their oaths during the independence movement.
story: The left ankle of Sati is said to have fallen here, and the site is linked in local tradition to Bhima of the Mahabharata.

name: Mangal Chandika Temple, Kogram (Ujani Shakti Pitha)
deity: Chandi (Mangal Chandika)
significance: The Chandi shrine at Kogram in Mangalkot block, identified with the ancient merchant settlement of Ujani and counted among the 51 Shakta pithas. The temple also preserves an old image of the Buddha and once held a statue of the Jain tirthankara Shantinatha.
story: A piece of the right arm-bend of Sati is said to have fallen at Kogram.

name: Narmada Temple, Amarkantak (Shondesh Shakti Pitha)
deity: Narmada, goddess of the river
significance: The principal temple of Amarkantak, standing at the source of the Narmada, built by the Kalachuris of Tripuri in the 12th century and later renovated by Maharani Ahilyabai Holkar. Amarkantak, where three major rivers rise, is described in Hindu scripture as the king of pilgrimages.
story: Adi Shankaracharya is said to have settled the dispute over the river's true source by declaring the stream at the temple to be the Narmada's mainstream.

name: Tungnath Temple
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as his arms
significance: At about 3,680 m this is one of the highest Shiva temples in the world and the third shrine of the Panch Kedar circuit in Uttarakhand. Adi Shankara is credited with setting its priestly traditions in the 8th century.
story: Fleeing the Pandavas after the Kurukshetra war, Shiva took the form of a bull that broke apart when Bhima seized it, and his arms surfaced at Tungnath.

name: Rudranath Temple
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as his face
significance: A Shiva shrine at roughly 3,600 m in the Garhwal Himalaya where the face of the god is worshipped, forming the fourth temple of the Panch Kedar circuit. It is also a site for ancestral rites.
story: When Bhima caught the bull into which Shiva had transformed, it sank into the ground and reappeared in five parts, the face emerging at Rudranath.

name: Madhyamaheshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as his navel and belly
significance: A Shiva temple at about 3,497 m in the Garhwal Himalaya of Uttarakhand and one of the five shrines of the Panch Kedar pilgrimage. Its design resembles those at Kedarnath and Tungnath.
story: The navel and stomach of the bull-form of Shiva are said to have surfaced here after the animal broke apart in Bhima's grasp.

name: Kalpeshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as his matted hair (jata)
significance: A Shiva temple at about 2,200 m in the Urgam valley, the fifth of the Panch Kedar shrines and the only one open to pilgrims all year. Its priestly line was appointed by Adi Shankara.
story: The matted locks of the bull-form of Shiva are said to have appeared at Kalpeshwar, where the Pandavas then raised a temple.

name: Jageshwar Temples
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Vishnu, Shakti goddesses and Surya
style: Nagara (North Indian), with Valabhi and latina variants
significance: A Himalayan group of more than 125 stone temples in Almora district, dated between the 7th and 14th centuries and protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Long a centre of Pashupata Shaivism, the cluster is unusual in that many shrines appear to be memorials rather than working places of worship.

name: Baijnath Temple, Uttarakhand
deity: Shiva as Vaidyanatha, lord of physicians
significance: A 12th-century Katyuri temple complex on the bank of the Gomati in Bageshwar district, now a Monument of National Importance and a stop on the Shiva Heritage Circuit. Besides Shiva it houses images of Parvati, Ganesha, Chandika, Kubera, Surya and Brahma.
story: Shiva and Parvati are said to have been married at the confluence of the Gomati and the Garur Ganga here.

name: Katarmal Sun Temple
deity: Surya, worshipped here as Burhadita (Vraddhaditya)
style: Katyuri stone construction with carved wooden doors and panels
significance: A rare 9th-century temple to the sun god in Almora district, built by the Katyuri king Katarmalla and surrounded by 44 smaller shrines. It is a Monument of National Importance protected under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act of 1958.

name: Manibandh Shaktipeeth (Gayatri Temple, Pushkar)
deity: Gayatri (Bhairava: Sarvanand)
significance: One of the 51 Shakta pithas, standing at the foot of Gayatri hill (Puruhuta) beside Pushkar, roughly 11 km north-west of Ajmer. It is venerated as the place where the wrists of Sati came to rest.
story: When Vishnu's discus scattered Sati's body across the subcontinent to end Shiva's grief, her wrists (manibandh) fell on this hill.
